title: How Long Does the IRS Have to Collect? (Infographic)
alt: The IRS has 10 years to collect Infographic from tax attorney Darrin Mish.
body:
Tax attorney Darrin Mish put this one-page guide together from official sources. Save it, print it or share it with someone who needs it.

What the infographic says

The IRS has 10 years to collect The clock starts when the tax is assessed, and each assessment has its own date. Some events pause the clock or add time to it.

  • The basic rule: 10 years. The IRS can collect by levy or lawsuit only within 10 years after it assesses the tax. When the period ends, so does its right to collect.
  • Asking for a payment plan. The clock pauses while your request is pending, for 30 days after a rejection or termination, and during an appeal.
  • Offering to settle (offer in compromise). The clock pauses while the offer is pending, for 30 days after a rejection, and during a timely appeal.
  • Asking for a Collection Due Process hearing. The clock pauses from the time the IRS gets your timely request until the decision is final, including court appeals.
  • Filing bankruptcy. The clock pauses while the IRS is barred from collecting, plus 6 more months.
  • Living outside the U.S. for 6 months or more. The clock pauses while you are away. It cannot run out until at least 6 months after you come back.
  • Other events. An innocent spouse request, combat zone service, military deferment, or a government lawsuit to collect can also stop or extend the clock.

If two events overlap, the paused time counts only once.

Sources

  • https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title26/html/USCODE-2024-title26-subtitleF-chap66-subchapA-sec6502.htm
  • https://www.irs.gov/irm/part5/irm_05-001-019
  • https://www.irs.gov/payments/payment-plans-installment-agreements
  • https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title26/html/USCODE-2024-title26-subtitleF-chap66-subchapA-sec6503.htm

Checked October 2026.

title: IRS Lien vs. Levy: What's the Difference? (Infographic)
alt: Lien or levy? Infographic from tax attorney Darrin Mish.
body:
Tax attorney Darrin Mish put this one-page guide together from official sources. Save it, print it or share it with someone who needs it.

What the infographic says

Lien or levy? They are not the same. A lien is a claim against your property. A levy actually takes it. Here is how the IRS explains each one.

Federal tax lien

  • What it is: The government's legal claim against your property when you neglect or fail to pay a tax debt.
  • When it arises: After the IRS assesses the tax, sends you a bill, and you neglect or refuse to pay in full in time.
  • What it covers: All your assets, including real estate, vehicles and financial assets, and assets you get later.
  • Public notice: The IRS may file a public Notice of Federal Tax Lien to alert creditors. It may limit your ability to get credit.
  • Getting it released: The IRS releases the lien within 30 days after you pay the tax debt in full.

IRS levy

  • What it is: A legal seizure of your property to satisfy a tax debt.
  • What it can take: Wages, bank accounts, retirement accounts, commissions, your car, your house and other property.
  • Before a levy: Usually a tax bill, then a Final Notice of Intent to Levy and Notice of Your Right to A Hearing at least 30 days before.
  • Wages: A wage levy is continuous. A portion of your wages is exempt.
  • Bank accounts: Funds are held, and after 21 days they are sent to the IRS.

The Final Notice of Intent to Levy also tells you about your right to a hearing. Act before the deadline on your letter.

Sources

  • https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/understanding-a-federal-tax-lien
  • https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/what-is-a-levy
  • https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/levy

Checked October 2026.

title: Can't Pay the IRS? Three Options Explained (Infographic)
alt: Can't pay? Three IRS options Infographic from tax attorney Darrin Mish.
body:
Tax attorney Darrin Mish put this one-page guide together from official sources. Save it, print it or share it with someone who needs it.

What the infographic says

Can't pay? Three IRS options How the IRS describes each option and who it fits.

Payment plan (installment agreement)

  • What it is: An agreement with the IRS to pay what you owe over an extended time.
  • Who it fits: People who can pay the full balance within that extended time.
  • Short term: Pay in 180 days or less.
  • Long term: Pay in monthly payments.
  • Keep in mind: Penalties and interest keep adding up until the balance is paid in full.

Offer in compromise

  • What it is: A way to settle your tax debt for less than the full amount you owe.
  • Who it fits: People who can't pay in full, or for whom paying would cause financial hardship.
  • The IRS looks at: Your income, expenses and the equity in your assets.
  • To qualify: File all required returns, make required estimated payments, and not be in an open bankruptcy.
  • Keep in mind: The IRS generally won't accept an offer if you can pay in full through a payment plan or asset equity.

Currently Not Collectible

  • What it is: The IRS temporarily delays most collection until your finances improve.
  • Who it fits: People who cannot pay because of financial hardship.
  • The IRS may ask: For financial forms and proof of income, living expenses, bank accounts and assets.
  • Keep in mind: You still owe the full amount. Penalties and interest continue. The IRS may file a lien and will apply your refunds to the debt.

Sources

  • https://www.irs.gov/payments/payment-plans-installment-agreements
  • https://www.irs.gov/payments/offer-in-compromise
  • https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/temporarily-delay-the-collection-process

title: Is It Really the IRS? Five Scam Red Flags (Infographic)
alt: Is it really the IRS? Infographic from tax attorney Darrin Mish.
body:
Tax attorney Darrin Mish put this one-page guide together from official sources. Save it, print it or share it with someone who needs it.

What the infographic says

Is it really the IRS? The IRS says a call, email or text is not from the IRS if it does any of the first five things below.

  • It comes out of the blue. The contact is unexpected.
  • It rushes you. You are pushed to act right now.
  • It threatens you. Scammers threaten arrest or deportation and won't let you question or appeal the amount.
  • It asks for personal or financial information. Do not give it out to an unexpected caller, email or text.
  • It demands payment now. Impersonators want you to pay "now or else."
  • How the IRS really contacts you. First contact is normally a letter by U.S. mail. The IRS emails or texts only if you opted in. A social media direct message is never from the IRS.
  • If someone shows up at your door. Visits are rare, and a letter usually comes first. Revenue officers and agents carry two IRS IDs you can ask to see.
  • Got a fake IRS email?. Don't click links or open attachments. Send it to phishing@irs.gov, then delete it.

Sources

  • https://www.irs.gov/help/how-to-know-its-the-irs
  • https://www.irs.gov/help/tax-scams/recognize-tax-scams-and-fraud
  • https://www.irs.gov/help/report-fraud/report-fake-irs-treasury-or-tax-related-emails-and-messages

title: Can Bankruptcy Wipe Out Income Tax? The 3-2-240 Rules (Infographic)
alt: Can bankruptcy wipe out income tax? Infographic from tax attorney Darrin Mish.
body:
Tax attorney Darrin Mish put this one-page guide together from official sources. Save it, print it or share it with someone who needs it.

What the infographic says

Can bankruptcy wipe out income tax? Sometimes. The Bankruptcy Code sets timing tests. Each tax year is tested on its own, counting back from the day you file bankruptcy.

  • The 3-year rule. The return's due date, including extensions, must be more than 3 years before you file bankruptcy.
  • The 2-year rule. You must have filed the return. If you filed it late, you must have filed it more than 2 years before you file bankruptcy.
  • The 240-day rule. The IRS must have assessed the tax more than 240 days before you file bankruptcy. Tax not yet assessed generally does not qualify.
  • Fraud or evasion blocks it. Tax is not discharged if you filed a fraudulent return or willfully tried to evade or defeat the tax.
  • An IRS-prepared return does not count. A substitute return the IRS makes for you under IRC 6020(b) is not treated as your return.
  • The clocks can be paused. A pending offer in compromise, a prior bankruptcy, or a collection hearing and appeal can extend these time periods.

Meeting the timing tests does not guarantee a discharge. Other conditions apply, so have your transcripts reviewed before you file.

Sources

  • https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title11/html/USCODE-2024-title11-chap5-subchapI-sec507.htm
  • https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title11/html/USCODE-2024-title11-chap5-subchapII-sec523.htm

title: Who Gets Audited? IRS Audit Rates by Income (Infographic)
alt: Who gets audited? Infographic from tax attorney Darrin Mish.
body:
Tax attorney Darrin Mish put this one-page guide together from official sources. Save it, print it or share it with someone who needs it.

What the infographic says

Who gets audited? Share of individual returns for tax year 2021 that the IRS had examined or was examining, by total positive income. Overall: 0.3%.

  • No total positive income: 1.8%
  • $1 to under $25,000: 0.5%
  • $25,000 to under $50,000: 0.2%
  • $50,000 to under $75,000: 0.2%
  • $75,000 to under $100,000: 0.2%
  • $100,000 to under $200,000: 0.2%
  • $200,000 to under $500,000: 0.2%
  • $500,000 to under $1 million: 0.6%
  • $1 million to under $5 million: 0.9%
  • $5 million to under $10 million: 3.9%
  • $10 million or more: 6.6%

Percent of returns filed, counting closed and in-process exams as of September 30, 2025.

Tax year 2021 is the most recent year outside the normal time limit for audits, so these rates are less likely to change. Total positive income adds up income sources and leaves out losses.

Sources

  • https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-soi/25db-3-01-ex.xlsx
  • https://www.irs.gov/statistics/soi-tax-stats-irs-data-book
